newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian paper confirms Vukovar atrocities.
newsitem.headline: Serbian paper confirms Vukovar atrocities.

text.p: Serbian media with close ties to the Belgrade government confirmed for the first time on Monday that Serb soldiers committed atrocities after the fall of the Croatian city of Vukovar in 1991.

The Belgrade newspaper "Dnevni Telegraf" published a story quoting an unnamed reservist in the Yugoslav army who said he saw drunken Serbian paramilitaries rob and beat Croatian men before taking them off to be executed outside of Vukovar.
Under the front page headline, "Eyewitness Testimony to Horror in Ovcara", the story confirmed charges that the Yugoslav government had vigorously denied in the past.

The International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia (ICTY) has indicted Colonel Veselin Sljivancanin and two other senior Yugoslav army officers for the massacre of more than 200 men in the village of Ovcara.
United Nations officials in Zagreb said on October 7 that investigators had found 200 bodies in a mass grave in Ovcara.
Analysts said the Belgrade newspaper report was the latest signal that Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic could bow to international pressure and eventually hand over the war crimes suspects.
"This may be a sign that Milosevic is preparing the ground for extraditing Sljivancanin," said Dejan Anastasijevic, a journalist with the Belgrade independent weekly Vreme.

Consolidating his power after the end of the Yugoslav conflict, Milosevic has been steadily purging the political and military leadership of those with links to wartime conquests and notorious "ethnic cleansing" operations.

Paramilitary chief Dragoslav Bokan, who has been accused of orchestrating expulsions and looting in Croatia and Bosnia early in the war, was arrested over the weekend on charges of robbing a man in the Serbian town of Novi Sad, Belgrade media reported.
Analysts said Bokan's arrest was almost certainly part of the post-war purge directed by Milosevic.

The Belgrade newspaper account of Ovcara described bloodthirsty paramilitaries committing atrocities against Croats in Vukovar but steered well clear from implicating rank and file members of the army.

Tribunal prosecutors have accused the Yugoslav army as well as paramilitary troops of committing war crimes in Vukovar but Belgrade pro-government media have been careful not to soil the name of the Yugoslav army.
Some analysts say Belgrade may seek a way out by choosing to accuse Sljivancanin and other Yugoslav officers of merely failing to control the paramilitaries.
The army reservist told the newspaper he was horrified by what he saw but said his unit would have been certainly killed as well if anyone had tried to protect the victims.
"I maintain that they were so drunk and crazed that they would have opened fire on us had we intervened and that would have done nothing to save the prisoners," he said.

ICTY prosecutors in the Hague say Serb forces removed wounded Croat patients, hospital staff, soldiers and political activists from Vukovar's hospital on November 20, 1991, after a devastating three-month siege.
Serb forces then shot some 260 men and bulldozed them into a mass grave, prosecutors say.
The source said 40 drunk and "crazed" paramilitaries robbed, beat and tormented up to 500 captured Croats, which included a small number of women.
One paramilitary beat an Albanian to death, another crushed a man's skull with his rifle butt and a third repeatedly kicked a pregnant woman in the stomach, the reservist said.
Several hours later the paramilitaries drove the prisoners to a small forest and the army unit withdrew to avoid any association with the "liquidation", the source said.
"I know they were prisoners from the basement of the Vukovar hosptial. There were wounded among them, but I am sure there were more than 200 of them.
"After we left we heard shooting until about one (hour) after midnight."
